title: Should Students Sit in Rows
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues against binary answers to classroom seating debates, making the case for row-and-pair seating in his own room based on the specific mix of learning tasks his students do rather than ideology about what seating signals. He recounts abandoning four-person pods after noticing students needed to spend cognitive effort resisting distraction from peers facing them during writing, reading, and direct instruction, a tax he says outweighed any community benefit. He directly rebuts the common charge that row seating is industrial, militaristic, or teacher-centered, noting he observed colleagues running highly engaging, warmly communal, humanizing classrooms in row formats. His conclusion is explicitly conditional: rows work in his room because his students' most frequent activities are best supported by minimizing distraction and maximizing sightlines, while structures like Think-Pair-Share and Pop-up Debate still provide daily peer interaction. He frames the whole piece as a caution against either-or thinking in pedagogical decisions.
points: Rejects should students sit in rows as a false binary, arguing the right answer depends on the specific mix of tasks a given classroom does most often.
Cites a specific cognitive-load cost of pod seating, students expending effort to ignore peers facing them, as the practical reason he abandoned it, not an ideological objection to group work.
Directly challenges the assumption that row seating is inherently militaristic or teacher-centered by pointing to colleagues running row-seated classrooms that were highly engaging and communal.
Preserves peer interaction within a row layout via specific structures (Think-Pair-Share, Conversation Challenge, Pop-up Debate) rather than treating rows and collaboration as mutually exclusive.
quotes: Engagement isn't something you can infer from smiling faces or a classroom arrangement. Engagement is what the brain attends to.

I used to have students sit in groups of four, facing each other in pods. I found this sub-optimal, mainly because too many of my students were needing to exert too much effort too much of the time to focus on something besides the folks they were sitting at the table with.
Anti-row folks would say that in such a room, students are being treated like industrial widgets. Community cannot be fostered in such a room. Such a seating format is militaristic or prison-like.

But then I started noticing row-seating classrooms run by competent colleagues in which the classroom vibe was highly engaging, warmly communal, and deeply humanizing. In fact, they were much more so than my own group-seating room was.

In other words, it turned out that the seating chart wasn't the deal-maker or the deal-breaker. As comforting as either-or thinking can be with its black-and-white certainties, pedagogical decisions often resists dogmatic oversimplification.
So, should your students sit in rows? My answer is that it depends on what kind of work they're most often going to be doing.
